results.api: Ndk.requests.query(filter, explicitRelays: [relay]).stream (closes after EOSE), one relay
results.crypto: libsecp256k1 (C, via rust secp256k1 0.31 in ndk's librust_lib_ndk.so, built by its build hook)
results.notes: Event verifier: RustEventVerifier() (Rust via FFI: id hash + BIP-340 in one native call). Every event goes through VerifyEventStream: Nip01Utils.isIdValid (Dart id recompute + NIP-13 PoW check) and the verifier; invalid events are dropped. It keeps an LRU of verified id/sig pairs per Ndk instance (a new Ndk per run, so nothing is reused across runs). Frames are JSON-decoded on an encoding isolate. NdkConfig: bootstrapRelays = [the relay] (connected and awaited in setup, untimed), MemCacheManager (a required parameter), log level off, and query timeout = 1 h (the default 10 s query timeout would cut the stream). The stream closes when the relay sends EOSE: that is the EOSE time. query(cacheRead: false, cacheWrite: false): with cacheWrite off ndk returns the verified stream as is, so nothing is stored (the defaults run in the ndk-cache variant). Expired events and older kind-0 versions are delivered. Library costs paid on every event, named not worked around: the id is computed twice (isIdValid in Dart, then again in the native call), the NIP-13 check, the frame's string length taken for relay stats, the query's returnedIds dedup set; and after connect ndk fires an unawaited NIP-11 HTTP GET (setup, but it may still be in flight). Nip01Event's constructor replaces created_at: 0 with the current time, so that valid event fails its id check and is dropped: accepted_ok is false.

Variant: query() with its defaults, cacheRead: true and cacheWrite: true: every verified event is saved to the MemCacheManager (saveEventIfAbsent, addEventSources) and then delivered only if loadEvents (with its visibility rules) still returns it, so expired events and a kind-0 profile older than another by the same author in the stream are dropped. Same as ndk-rust otherwise. Library costs paid on every event, named not worked around: the id is computed twice (isIdValid in Dart, then again in the native call), the NIP-13 check, the frame's string length taken for relay stats, the query's returnedIds dedup set; and after connect ndk fires an unawaited NIP-11 HTTP GET (setup, but it may still be in flight). EventRepositoryImpl drops events whose signature fails (EventModel.isValid = bip340.verify(pubkey, id, sig)) but never checks the id. Who does which half: the signature is the library's (in its stream); the id half is the library's own Event.calculateId(...) (jsonEncode + SHA-256), called by the harness on every delivered event, inside the run, comparing with the id field and dropping mismatches (as go-nostr's CheckID; verify stays library). The repositories are wired the way SubscribeUseCase does it, minus the use case (it hides the EOSE stream).

A new Nostr() instance per run (Nostr.instance is a process-wide singleton whose registry drops event ids it has seen before). Slow pass: one timed run, measured after a container restart on a slower host: the go-nostr-relay control took 8,547 ms there against 7,881 ms in the main pass (+8 %), so compare this row with the others only to within ~10 %. Last release 2023. The relay stream delivers every event unverified (the verifying Event constructor body is commented out): per event the harness calls EventApi().getEventHash(event) (the library's id function) against event.id, then EventApi().verifySignature(event) (BIP-340). results.api: Nostr().pool.add(Relay(url)) + await pool.subscribe([filter], onEvent) (returns at EOSE), one relay
results.notes: Slow pass: one timed run, measured after a container restart on a slower host: the go-nostr-relay control took 8,547 ms there against 7,881 ms in the main pass (+8 %), so compare this row with the others only to within ~10 %. Last release 2023. RelayPool verifies every event (Event.isValid: id recomputed; Event.isSigned: BIP-340; signature verification is on unless Nostr(disableSignatureVerification: true)). The pool hides EOSE, but pool.subscribe() awaits the relay's ack, which is the EOSE: its return is the EOSE time. Relay.connect() needs NIP-11 over https and NIPs 15+20 listed, so Relay gets a RelayInfoProvider (its public constructor parameter) that returns {supported_nips: [1, 11, 15, 20]}. Caveat: the ack wait has a hard-coded 1 min timeout that disconnects the relay, so a subscription whose EOSE takes longer than 1 min to process is cut off. Relay.connect() starts IOWebSocketChannel.connect without awaiting the handshake (the channel is private), so setup waits 200 ms after pool.add (untimed), as for nostr_tools and nostr_client. It pins bip340 ^0.0.4 (as nostr_client and nostr_dart do), whose verify serializes the public key with bigToBytes (helpers.dart:12, no left padding): for a pubkey whose first byte is 0 the BIP-340 challenge hashes 31 bytes and the valid signature fails, so every event from such a key is dropped (83 in the full corpus; fixed in bip340 0.2.0, which the ^0.0.4 constraint excludes).

The relay stream delivers raw jsonDecoded messages; the harness turns EVENT messages into the library's Event with Event.fromJson and calls event.verify() (BIP-340 over the id, the library's only check). results.websocket: dart:io WebSocket (the library has no relay client; its examples use dart:io WebSocket)
results.notes: The library has no WebSocket client ("transport-agnostic"), so this is a variant paired with dart:io WebSocket as in its examples. Message.deserialize parses each frame; for an EVENT it builds the Event with the default verify: true, which recomputes the id and checks the BIP-340 signature and throws on failure (counted as rejected). Library cost, named not worked around: each EVENT frame is JSON-decoded twice, once by Message.deserialize (to read the message type) and again by Event.deserialize on the same frame string.

EventRepositoryImpl drops events whose signature fails (EventModel.isValid = bip340.verify(pubkey, id, sig)) but never checks the id. Who does which half: the signature is the library's (in its stream); the id half is the library's own Event.calculateId(...) (jsonEncode + SHA-256), called by the harness on every delivered event, inside the run, comparing with the id field and dropping mismatches (as go-nostr's CheckID; verify stays library). The repositories are wired the way SubscribeUseCase does it, minus the use case (it hides the EOSE stream).

results.crypto: bip340 0.3.1 + pointycastle 4.0.0 (pure Dart, on compute isolates)
results.notes: Event verifier: Bip340EventVerifier() (the documented default: pure Dart, verifies on a compute isolate). Every event goes through VerifyEventStream: Nip01Utils.isIdValid (Dart id recompute + NIP-13 PoW check) and the verifier; invalid events are dropped. It keeps an LRU of verified id/sig pairs per Ndk instance (a new Ndk per run, so nothing is reused across runs). Frames are JSON-decoded on an encoding isolate. NdkConfig: bootstrapRelays = [the relay] (connected and awaited in setup, untimed), MemCacheManager (a required parameter), log level off, and query timeout = 1 h (the default 10 s query timeout would cut the stream). The stream closes when the relay sends EOSE: that is the EOSE time. query(cacheRead: false, cacheWrite: false): with cacheWrite off ndk returns the verified stream as is, so nothing is stored (the defaults run in the ndk-cache variant). Expired events and older kind-0 versions are delivered. Library costs paid on every event, named not worked around: the id is computed twice (isIdValid in VerifyEventStream and again inside Bip340EventVerifier.verify), the NIP-13 check, the frame's string length taken for relay stats, the query's returnedIds dedup set; and after connect ndk fires an unawaited NIP-11 HTTP GET (setup, but it may still be in flight). Nip01Event's constructor replaces created_at: 0 with the current time, so that valid event fails its id check and is dropped: accepted_ok is false.
